title: You Maxed Out Your 401(k) at $24,500. Could a Mega Backdoor Roth Let You Save Up to $47,500 More in 2026?
summary: A mega backdoor Roth can let workers who max out their 401(k) contribute after-tax money and convert it to Roth savings.
body_markdown:
If you[maxed out your 401(k)](https://smartasset.com/retirement/maxed-out-401k-and-still-had-room-this-move-added-40k-in-tax-free-savings) in 2026, you may be wondering whether there’s another way to save more for retirement. Depending on the rules of your plan, you might be able to use a[mega backdoor Roth](https://smartasset.com/retirement/mega-backdoor-roth) to save beyond the 401(k) limit. Here’s how you could save up to $47,500 more before 2026 comes to an end.


## Adding $47,500 to Your Nest Egg After Maxing Out a 401(k)


The IRS sets two key limits for 401(k) plans. In 2026, you can[contribute up to $24,500](https://smartasset.com/retirement/maximum-401k-contributions) from your paycheck, while total annual additions to your account may not exceed either $72,000 or 100% of your pay, whichever is less.1 This includes your own contributions, any[employer matches](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-does-401k-match-work) and certain after-tax contributions. In 2027, the employee limit will go up to $25,500 and the overall limit to $75,000.2


The gap between those two limits is the space a[mega backdoor Roth](https://smartasset.com/retirement/mega-backdoor-roth-limit) can use. The table shows how that space fills up each year without any employer contributions:


Contribution Category 2026 Amount 2027 Amount


Overall limit $72,000 $75,000


Employee contribution $24,500 $25,500


Employer contribution $0 $0


Potential after-tax contribution $47,500 $49,500


[Employer matches](https://smartasset.com/retirement/how-roth-401k-matching-works-with-your-employer) change the calculation, since they count toward the same overall limit. In that case, let’s assume that your employer contributes $10,000, your after-tax space shrinks by the same amount:


- **For 2026:** $72,000 − $24,500 − $10,000 = $37,500
- **For 2027:** $75,000 − $25,500 − $10,000 = $39,500

## If You’re 50 or Older, You Can Save at Least $8,000 More


Workers 50 and older can make[catch-up contributions](https://smartasset.com/retirement/all-about-catch-up-contributions) on top of the regular 401(k) limit. In 2026, the catch-up limit is $8,000, and workers ages 60 to 63 can make a larger[super catch-up contribution](https://smartasset.com/retirement/super-catch-up-secure-2-0) of up to $11,250. For 2027, those limits rise to $8,500 and $11,750.


Catch-up contributions don’t count toward the overall limit, so they don’t use up any of the space for a mega backdoor Roth. That means a worker 50 or older could take three steps in the same year, as long as the plan allows them:


- **Max out regular contributions:** $24,500 in 2026; $25,500 in 2027
- **Add catch-up contributions:** $8,000 ($11,250 for those ages 60 to 63) in 2026; $8,500 and $11,750 in 2027
- **Make after-tax contributions:** Up to $47,500 in 2026; $49,500 in 2027


The table shows the most a worker could contribute in total each year, assuming that they don’t have an employer match:


Age 2026 Total 2027 Total


Under 50 $72,000 $75,000


50 to 59, or 64 and older $80,000 $83,500


60 to 63 $83,250 $86,750


To see how those totals add up, here’s a comparison of the limits that a 61-year-old could save in 2026 and 2027 without employer contributions:


Contribution Type 2026 2027


Regular contributions $24,500 $25,500


Super catch-up contributions $11,250 $11,750


After-tax contributions $47,500 $49,500


Total $83,250 $86,750


Higher earners should know about one more rule. Starting in 2026, workers who earned more than $150,000 from their employer in the previous year must put their catch-up contributions into a[Roth account](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-a-roth-ira) .3 That won’t reduce how much you can save, but that money get taxed upfront.


## Why Timing Matters Before 2026 Ends


[401(k) contributions](https://smartasset.com/retirement/maximum-401k-contributions) count toward the year in which they come out of your paycheck, so any after-tax contributions for 2026 generally have to be made through payroll by your last paycheck of the year. Unlike[an IRA](https://smartasset.com/retirement/what-is-an-ira) , a 401(k) doesn’t let you make contributions for the previous year after December 31, and any unused space doesn’t carry over to 2027.


With only a few paychecks left in the year, the remaining space has to be spread across fewer pay periods. For example, if you wanted to contribute the full $47,500 over your last three biweekly paychecks, it would take about $15,833 of after-tax money from each one ($47,500 ÷ 3).


That’s only possible if your take-home pay can cover it and your plan allows a contribution rate that high. It’s worth noting that many plans cap the percentage you can contribute from each paycheck, and you may also have to give advance notice to change your contribution election.


A mega backdoor Roth can also help you save on taxes in a different way. Moving after-tax contributions to a Roth quickly can help you keep more of your savings later. Money in a Roth grows without being taxed, and you generally won’t owe anything on qualified withdrawals during retirement.
